This contradicts the header's "else the session id" (lines 11-13). Reproduced: sessions sessA and sessB both accrue to bd-old.jsonl.
head/.claude/hooks/quality/karpathy-surgical-diff-check.sh:10 — the header says totals are keyed by "the current task", but checkpoint.task is the last CLOSED bead (state-schemas.md; implementing-tasks/SKILL.md:211 writes it after `br close`). Lines written for task N+1 are credited to task N, and the SURGICAL review axis reads the wrong task. KS-1 fakes the ordering with an already-closed bead.
head/.claude/loa/reference/hooks-reference.md:271 — the docs say decision rows carry hook/action/decision/mode. The implement-gate claim ask/deny rows (implement-gate.sh:423-424) set `mode: "authoritative"` and put the real mode under `gate_mode`, and they and the trust-input row (implement-gate.sh:349) use `timestamp` and a raw `file_path` instead of `ts`/`path`. Consumers that group by `.mode` or `.ts` mis-bucket or drop them.
head/.claude/scripts/lib/profile-lib.sh:77 — GNU `stat -Lc` exits 1 if any operand is missing (no floor.yaml, or no .loa.config.yaml). The `||` fallback then runs `stat -Lf`, which on GNU means filesystem status, so the cache key is built from free-block and inode counts, not mtimes. Edits to the config are then served stale (reproduced: full→lean→full returned the same value each time) or the cache rebuilds on nearly every call. Stat only the existing files, or detect GNU vs BSD up front.
head/.claude/scripts/lib/profile-lib.sh:208 — both _loa_pl_load and the live-read fallback need jq. Under yq without jq, every explicitly set key returns the fallback. Before this change, loa-kf-surface.sh / loa-l7-surface-soul.sh needed only yq; an explicit `true` is now silently ignored. loa-decisions-surface.sh also loses its documented "jq is missing" warning (its header lines 11-12).
head/.claude/scripts/lib/profile-lib.sh:61 — LOA_PROFILE_CONFIG_FILE / LOA_PROFILES_FILE / LOA_PROFILE_FLOOR_FILE / LOA_PROFILE_ROOT / LOA_PROFILE_CACHE_FILE are honoured outside bats; only LOA_STATUS_CONFIG_FILE is gated (lines 58-60). The lib now feeds danger-level-enforcer.sh, guardrails-orchestrator.sh and the L6/L7 surfacing hooks, so one env var can switch off danger-level enforcement or input guardrails, or turn L7 surfacing on. That bypasses the hooks' own two-factor test gates and the kernel rule that test-mode env overrides are bats-gated.
head/.claude/data/profiles.yaml:42 — `standard` (the default profile) sets invisible_retrospective.enabled: true. Base ran the retrospective scan only on an explicit true. The oracle records false for this repo and for an empty config today (standard-oracle.json), and .loa.config.yaml does not set the key, so the silent post-skill scan is newly on for every user. The header (lines 14-15) lists only the two guardrail keys as default changes.
head/.loa.config.yaml.example:21 — the comment says `lean` turns these keys all off and `full` all on, but the example explicitly sets 8 of the 9 profile keys (lines 312, 325, 1358, 1404, 1432, 2932, 2950, 2962), and explicit keys beat the profile. For anyone starting from the example, `loa.profile: full`/`lean` changes only soul_identity_doc.enabled and reports five "explicit overrides" the user never chose. PL-4 (profile-lib.bats:76-78) locks this in.
Verdict: CHANGES_REQUIRED

content.text:
The pull request can't merge: my verdict is **CHANGES_REQUIRED**. The review is in `/workspace/review.md` (23 findings plus the verdict line), and nothing under `pr/` was changed.

I reviewed the heredoc classifier myself. Three parallel agents covered run position, the implement gate and surgical-diff hook, and profiles and tooling. I re-checked the most serious of their claims against the code before including them. The fence corpus passes on the head hook (benign 89/89, dangerous 142/142), so the problems below are cases the corpus doesn't cover.

**Blocking problems**
- **Heredoc classifier lets dangerous commands through.** The PR calls it "fail-closed", but the head hook now allows commands that the base hook blocks:
  - A heredoc written to `cmds.txt` and then run with `cat cmds.txt | bash` or `bash -c "$(cat cmds.txt)"` in the same command. The check that looks for the file being run elsewhere misses both forms (`block-destructive-bash.sh:631`).
  - A heredoc written to a `Makefile` and then run with `make`. Files that tools pick up by name are treated as plain data (`block-destructive-bash.sh:303`).

  In both cases the body's writes into `.claude/hooks/` or `.run/cron.d/` are no longer checked. I reproduced each one: base exits 2 (blocked), head exits 0 (allowed).
- **`run-checkpoint.sh derive` doesn't work on jq 1.6.** It uses `$label` as a variable name, which is a reserved word in jq 1.6, so `derive` always fails. Every `write` and `mark` also prints errors. I confirmed this with the system jq (1.6), which is still the default on Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 11. Renaming the variable fixes it.
- **Circuit-breaker logic in `run-checkpoint.sh` is broken in several ways:**
  - When no breaker file exists, the one it creates has no thresholds and no timeout start, so the timeout can never trip.
  - The documented `/run-resume --force` is undone by the very next checkpoint.
  - Old feedback files without a verdict trailer always look like "no progress", so the breaker trips even when the findings change.
  - A reset can race with a checkpoint write and be silently undone.
- **Implement gate can deny a live run.** The run check still uses a fixed 24 h limit while the run position uses `run_mode.stale_hours`. With deny mode and `stale_hours` above 24, a live run gets denied with a message that says the position is RUNNING. A new check also skips the older state files whenever the cache is stale, which the docs say should not happen.
- **Surgical-diff hook counts against the wrong task.** After any run finishes, every later session's lines accumulate under the old task. Separately, the counted task is the last *closed* one, not the current one.
- **Profiles library (`profile-lib.sh`):**
  - On Linux, if any input file is missing, the cache key is built from filesystem free-space numbers instead of file times, so config edits can be served stale.
  - Hooks that only needed yq now also need jq; without it, explicitly set options are silently ignored.
  - Its test-override environment variables work outside the test suite, so one variable can switch off danger-level enforcement.
  - The default `standard` profile quietly turns on the background retrospective scan for every user.
  - Because the example config sets most of these options explicitly, `lean` and `full` barely do anything for people who start from it.

I also listed a few tests that don't exercise what they claim, and a few places where the docs don't match the code.

**Not verified:**
- The jq 1.6 failure in `record-round` was reproduced by an agent using a second jq install; I didn't rerun it.
- Files outside the PR, such as `guard-yield.sh`, the real `floor.yaml` and `verdict-derive.sh`, aren't in the snapshot, so findings involving them were tested against stubs or read from the code only.
